To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Mealy dyke swarm in Labrador records a pre-Grenville event at 1000 ± 100 Ma.
the Mealy dyke swarm was emplaced in a paleomagnetic field that was similar to the present-day field, but rotated 90° counterclockwise.

(1) the Mealy dyke swarm is older than the Grenville event and (2) the dykes have a complex magnetic history, which includes a magnetization that was acquired during their emplacement at 1000 ± 50 Ma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the magnetism of the Mealy Dyke swarm.
the paleomagnetic history of a suite of dykes that intrude anorthositic rocks of the Mealy Mountains complex in Labrador.
the paleomagnetic record of the Mealy Dyke swarm in Labrador, Canada, and its implications for the tectonic evolution of the Grenville Province.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the magnetizations in the Mealy dyke complex are of Late Archean or Proterozoic age and that they were acquired during the emplacement of the dykes.
the Mealy dyke system was magnetically active prior to the Grenville event and that the magnetization was acquired at temperatures of about 300 °C.
the Mealy dyke magnetizations are not related to the Grenville event.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dykes are not older than the Grenville event and probably younger than 1000 Myr.
the Mealy dyke swarm was emplaced at about 1100 Ma, and that the dykes were cooled to about 400 °C before the Grenville orogeny.
the magnetic history of the Mealey dykes can be explained in terms of two magnetizations acquired during cooling from a magmatic temperature of about 1000 °C.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Grenville Front is not a simple tectonic boundary, but rather a region of deformation and complex thermal histories, and that it is possible to obtain reliable paleomagnetic directions in rocks from this region.
the dykes have been subjected to temperatures below the Curie point of magnetite since about 1000 Ma.
the Mealy dyke swarm was magnetized during the Grenvillian orogeny, and that the Grenvillian event was not a single event.
